title: Truth to power
hook: soft words for hard things: in Tilang, Guru Nanak speaks as the Word comes to him, to Lalo by name, and turns wedding words into plain words for killing

segments.voice: Yesterday, the women of Saidpur, remembered as brides before the hymn mourns them. Your line was he mourned them. Whose story did you tell, with her before included? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-one.

Official language has a gift for soft words. An incident. Unrest. A regrettable loss. A difficult period. Each one is true enough to say out loud and vague enough that nobody has to picture anything. Soft words protect someone. The question is who. Guru Nanak's hymn in Raga Tilang, on ang seven twenty-two, has no soft words in it at all. And it explains why in its very first line, spoken to a friend, Lalo, whom tradition remembers as a carpenter. Today: truth to power.
screen: `AN INCIDENT. UNREST. A LOSS.` → `SOFT WORDS PROTECT SOMEONE.` → `A HYMN WITH NO SOFT WORDS.`

segments.voice: First, the opening, in paraphrase: as the Word of the Master comes to me, so I speak it, Lalo. That's the hymn's whole method. It doesn't take the Word and polish it into something safer. It says it as it comes. Earlier on this path we heard this line as courage, and later as truth told at the time of truth. Today, listen for its plainness. Second, the refrain. Line after line ends with ve Lalo, O Lalo. The hymn keeps saying a name. Plain speech here isn't a speech to a crowd or a letter to a palace. It's said to one man, a working man as tradition remembers him, again and again, the way you'd talk to a friend across a table when something terrible has happened. Third, the words it chooses. Yesterday the lament remembered weddings. This hymn uses wedding words too, and turns them inside out. The invader comes like a wedding party, but a wedding party of sin. Wedding songs are sung, the hymn says, but they're songs of blood. And blood takes the place of the red powder a bride wears. Every pretty word you'd use for a celebration is dragged into the light and made to say exactly what happened. That's the opposite of a soft word. It's a familiar word forced to tell the truth. Fourth, what that asks of us. Speaking truth to power, here, isn't shouting. It's refusing to blur. Say the thing as it is, to the person in front of you, by name, kindly, and don't let the comfortable word cover it. Today's line: speak as it comes.
screen: `AS THE WORD COMES, SO I SPEAK.` · `VE LALO: SAID TO ONE FRIEND.` · `WEDDING WORDS, TURNED INSIDE OUT.` · `REFUSING TO BLUR.` · then, large: `SPEAK AS IT COMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one honest thing to say kindly. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've been describing to yourself in soft words: a fight that you keep calling a misunderstanding, a habit you keep calling a phase, a hurt you keep calling nothing. Find the plain word for it. Then think of the one person it belongs to, and shape a single sentence that's both true and kind. Don't say it yet. Just hold it, and notice that it can be held. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. The bell holds the time.
Truth to power. Guru Nanak's Tilang hymn to Lalo: as the Master's Word comes, so I speak, in plain words that turn wedding songs into songs of blood. Today's word.
Your line: speak as it comes. Today, catch one soft word you'd normally reach for, and use the plain one instead, kindly, to the person it's meant for. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing this Tilang shabad addressed to Bhai Lalo in kirtan, and its opening line about speaking as the Master's Word comes is cited as a model for honest, fearless speech.

trapdoor: what you thought: speaking truth to power means shouting at kings.
what it means: in this hymn it means refusing to blur, said plainly to a friend by name, as the Word comes.
what a scholar hears: the refrain ve laalo, and wedding words turned over: janj, a wedding party of sin; sohile, wedding songs of blood.
